pages.cardTitle: Choosing polos for a team uniform
pages.cardBlurb: Fabric weight, piqué vs jersey, colours that survive the wash — the five decisions behind a polo order that lasts.
pages.h1: Choosing polos for a team uniform.
pages.metaTitle: Choosing Team Polo Shirts: The Buying Guide | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How to buy polos for a team — fabric weights and blends, piqué vs jersey, colour fastness, embroidery placement and the sizing spread that stops the second order going wrong.
pages.lede: The polo is the workhorse of team uniform — smart enough for customers, tough enough for the van. The difference between an order that looks sharp in month six and one that bags, fades and pills is five decisions made before you buy.

blocks.h2: Fabric first — weight and blend do the work
blocks.html:
Weight: workwear polos live around 180–220 gsm. Lighter feels flimsy and goes translucent in pale colours; heavier drinks money and dries slowly on the airer. Blend: poly-cotton (the classic 65/35) survives industrial washing and holds colour; cotton-rich feels nicer against skin but fades and shrinks faster; polyester-heavy wicks best for active roles at the cost of a synthetic hand-feel.

Knit: piqué — the textured waffle knit — is the uniform default: it holds its shape, hides minor wear, and takes embroidery beautifully. Smooth jersey reads more casual and shows embroidery pucker sooner. For teams, piqué wins on longevity almost every time.

head: Decision

rows: Cotton-rich if comfort outranks wash life

blocks.h2: Branding and sizing — where reorders go wrong
blocks.html:
Embroider, don't print, for chest logos on kit that's washed weekly — the comparison explains why — and keep the logo left-chest, 8–10 cm wide, clear of the placket. Sizing spread: order against real people, not a guess at averages, and buy one spare set per size band — teams change faster than uniform budgets renew. And check the maker offers a consistent colour across sizes and reorders; a subtly different navy on the new starter's polo undoes the uniform effect the order paid for.

Long-sleeve variants, ladies' cuts and hi-vis-adjacent colours all exist across the polo range — spec them at order time, not as an afterthought.

faq.q: What weight polo shirt is best for work?
faq.a: 180–220 gsm is the workwear window — substantial enough to keep shape and stay opaque, light enough to wear year-round and dry overnight. Below about 170 gsm, pale colours go translucent and the polo reads as promotional rather than uniform.

faq.q: What's the difference between piqué and jersey polos?
faq.a: Piqué is the textured knit — it holds structure, hides wear and takes embroidery cleanly, which makes it the uniform default. Jersey is smooth and softer but shows pucker around stitching and reads more casual.

faq.q: How many polos does each team member need?
faq.a: Three to five each depending on wash frequency — enough that a mid-week disaster doesn't put a stained polo in front of a customer. Order a spare set per size band; new starters never arrive in convenient sizes.

blocks.h2: Knee-pad pockets are a certification, not a gimmick
blocks.html:
Trousers with knee-pad pockets pair with foam inserts under EN 14404 — the knee-protection standard, certified as trousers-plus-pads together. For kneeling trades (flooring, tiling, joinery, groundworks) this is the single highest-value feature on the garment: the knees are the career-length decision. Two details matter at order time: top-loading pockets hold pads in place better through a working day, and pads are consumables — order spares with the trousers.

Fabric and construction carry the rest: 240–300+ gsm poly-cotton or ripstop for trade wear, triple-stitched seams at the seat and inside leg, and bar-tacks at pocket corners. Lighter stretch fabrics are genuinely better for active fitting work — but check the weight; slim cuts sold on comfort can be summer-weight cloth wearing trade styling.

faq.q: What's the difference between cargo and holster trousers?
faq.a: Cargo trousers carry volume in fixed thigh pockets; holster trousers hang external pockets you can load with fixings and tools for fast access — a joiner's and electrician's favourite. Holsters win for speed, cargos for bulk, and many trades run both by task.

faq.q: What is EN 14404?
faq.a: The knee-protection standard — certified as a system of trousers plus foam knee-pad inserts. If your work involves kneeling, trousers with certified pad pockets (and pads actually in them) are the highest-value feature you can buy.

faq.q: Are stretch work trousers durable enough for site?
faq.a: Good ones are — elastane-blend ripstops at proper weights handle site work while following the knee. The check is fabric weight: some slim styles are summer-weight cloth with trade styling. For heavy trades, look at 260 gsm upward or reinforced panels.

pages.cardTitle: Thermals & base layers guide
pages.cardBlurb: The layer that does the real winter work — synthetic vs merino, fit rules, and why cotton is banned from the list.
pages.h1: Base layers: the cheapest warmth you can buy.
pages.metaTitle: Thermals & Base Layers for Work: Buying Guide | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How base layers actually keep outdoor workers warm — synthetic vs merino, the snug-fit rule, cotton's ban, and matching the layer to site work, cold stores and winter driving.
pages.lede: Crews spend hundreds on jackets and pounds on base layers — backwards, since the layer against your skin decides whether sweat becomes warmth or chill. It's the highest warmth-per-pound purchase in workwear, if you follow three rules.

blocks.html:
A working body sweats even in January. Whatever sits against the skin either moves that moisture outward — keeping the insulating layers dry and working — or holds it, and wet fabric conducts heat away many times faster than dry. That's the entire base-layer job, and it's why cotton is banned from this list: it absorbs sweat, stays wet, and turns into a refrigeration layer at the first tea break. The classic cotton tee under a site jacket is the most common self-inflicted cold on British sites.

Fit is function: a base layer wicks by touching skin — snug through the torso and arms, not compression-tight, never baggy. If it hangs loose it's just a thin shirt.

head: Synthetic (polyester/polypropylene)
Merino wool
rows: Slower to dry, warm even damp
Multi-day wear, moderate output, sensitive skin
No — synthetics melt. FR-rated or natural layers only

blocks.h2: Matching the layer to the work
blocks.html: Outdoor trades: lightweight synthetic top and leggings under normal workwear — warmth without bulk under the site layering system. Cold stores: the base layer is load-bearing kit under an EN 342 suit — wicking matters more there than anywhere, because sweat inside a freezer suit is the classic failure. Drivers and yard staff: a mid-weight zip-neck covers the in-and-out pattern without overheating the cab. Anyone in FR: the melt-layer rule owns the decision — FR-rated or natural fibre only, T-shirt included.

faq.q: Why is cotton bad as a base layer?
faq.a: Cotton absorbs sweat and holds it against the skin, and wet fabric strips body heat many times faster than dry. A cotton tee under winter kit becomes a chilling layer by the first break — synthetic or merino wicking layers exist to prevent exactly that.

faq.q: Should a base layer be tight?
faq.a: Snug — in contact with skin through the torso and arms so it can wick — but not compression-tight. Baggy defeats the mechanism entirely; it's just a thin shirt with an insulating air gap it can't use.

faq.q: Are merino base layers worth it for work?
faq.a: For multi-day wear, moderate work rates and anyone bothered by synthetic odour, yes — merino stays wearable for days and insulates even damp. For daily-washed fleets doing sweaty work, synthetics wick faster, survive hot washing and cost half as much.

pages.cardBlurb: Past the green labels: recycled fabrics, the durability argument, and the questions that separate substance from marketing.
pages.h1: Sustainable workwear, past the green labels.
pages.metaTitle: Sustainable Workwear: An Honest Buying Guide | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: What sustainable workwear genuinely means — recycled polyester and organic cotton, why durability is the biggest lever, end-of-life reality, and the greenwash questions to ask.
pages.lede: Workwear has a genuine sustainability story and a lot of green paint. The genuine part: garments bought once, worn for years and kept in service beat almost any fabric claim. Here's how to buy it with a straight face.

blocks.html:
The most sustainable garment in your fleet is the one that doesn't get replaced this year. A heavier, better-constructed polo that survives three years of washing outperforms a recycled-fabric one binned in twelve months — on carbon, water and waste. So the hierarchy runs: buy durable → keep it in service (care and repair-adjacent maintenance) → then let fabric claims break ties.

On those claims: recycled polyester (rPET) is the workhorse — bottle-derived fibre with genuinely lower impact than virgin, now common in fleeces, polos and softshells at trade prices. Organic and better-cotton programmes cut pesticide and water impact on the cotton share of blends. Both are real; neither makes a flimsy garment sustainable.

blocks.h2: What a sustainable uniform programme actually does
blocks.html: Beyond the garments: rationalise the wardrobe (fewer, better lines beat a sprawling catalogue of cheap ones), embroider rather than print where possible so garments outlive design tweaks, rotate and launder properly so kit reaches its design life — most of the care hub is quietly a sustainability page — and plan end-of-life: de-branding and textile recycling for retired uniform rather than the skip. None of it is glamorous; all of it beats a leaf on a label.

faq.q: Is recycled polyester workwear actually better?
faq.a: Genuinely lower-impact than virgin polyester, yes — and now available at trade prices in fleeces, polos and shells. But the bigger lever is service life: a durable garment kept in use for years beats a short-lived recycled one on every environmental measure.

faq.q: What certifications should sustainable workwear have?
faq.a: Look for named schemes with numbers attached: GRS (Global Recycled Standard) or OCS for recycled content, OEKO-TEX for chemical safety, organic certification on cotton claims. An unquantified 'eco' label with no scheme behind it is marketing.

faq.q: What happens to old branded workwear?
faq.a: The responsible route is de-branding (unpicking or covering logos) and textile recycling or reuse schemes rather than landfill — some suppliers and laundries run take-back programmes. Planning it at purchase time beats improvising at skip time.

pages.metaDesc: Maternity workwear options by trimester and role — purpose-made ranges, adaptable sizing, maternity hi-vis, and the employer's duty to provide PPE that actually fits.
pages.lede: Workwear catalogues mostly pretend pregnancy doesn't happen — and pregnant workers end up in wrong-sized men's kit that fits nowhere and protects worse. Better options exist; here's the honest map of them.

heroMeta.l: An employer duty, not a favour

blocks.html:
The strongest purpose-made maternity ranges cluster where the most pregnant workers are: healthcare tunics and scrubs with expansion panels and adjustable sides, maternity work trousers and leggings with over-bump or under-bump waistbands, and — genuinely — maternity hi-vis: certified vests and jackets cut for a bump, because a standard vest riding open at the front loses its certified visible area exactly where drivers look. Office-adjacent uniform (shirts, dresses) borrows well from mainstream maternity wear with an embroidered layer over the top.

Where purpose-made runs out, adaptation beats up-sizing: buying a men's XXL just makes everything long and loose in the wrong places while staying tight in the one place that matters. Adjustable-waist designs, wrap styles, stretch fabrics and layering pieces (open softshells, cardigans in uniform colours) carry the middle months better.

blocks.html: The employer side is a duty, not a perk. UK employers must risk-assess work for new and expectant mothers, and PPE law requires equipment that fits the wearer — a vest that gapes open over a bump or boots that no longer fit swollen feet fail that test. Uniform and PPE reviews belong in the pregnancy risk assessment alongside task changes, and reassessment each trimester is the practical rhythm.

faq.q: Does maternity hi-vis exist?
faq.a: Yes — certified maternity hi-vis vests and jackets cut to stay closed over a bump, keeping the fluorescent area intact where a standard vest would gape open. For pregnant staff around vehicles, it's the correct answer rather than a bigger standard vest.

faq.q: Do employers have to provide maternity workwear?
faq.a: Employers must risk-assess work for new and expectant mothers, and PPE they provide must fit the wearer — which in practice means providing suitable maternity alternatives where standard kit no longer fits or protects. Uniform policy should follow the risk assessment.

faq.q: Can you just buy bigger sizes instead of maternity workwear?
faq.a: It rarely works — up-sizing adds length and shoulder width while staying wrong at the bump, and on PPE it can genuinely reduce protection (gaping hi-vis, trip-length trousers). Purpose-made or genuinely adjustable designs fit better and protect properly.

Sizing across a workforce: gloves in S–XL with the split learned from the first month's usage (a 1:2:2:1 ratio is a common starting spread), and dispensers stocked per zone so the right size is the near size.

faq.q: Are nitrile or vinyl gloves better?
faq.a: Nitrile for almost all working use — stronger, more puncture- and chemical-resistant, low allergy risk. Vinyl's place is brief, light, low-risk tasks where its lower price outweighs its fragility. Latex feels good but allergy risk has many workplaces banning it outright.

faq.q: Do disposable gloves expire?
faq.a: Yes — polymers age. Nitrile stiffens and loses elasticity, typically over a few years and much faster in heat and UV. Store boxes cool, dark and dry, rotate first-in-first-out, and treat brittle or discoloured gloves as expired.

faq.q: What sizes of disposable gloves should we stock?
faq.a: A spread from S to XL, weighted to your workforce — a 1:2:2:1 starting ratio is common, then adjust from real usage. Fit matters even on disposables: baggy gloves wreck dexterity and tight ones tear on donning.

pages.cardTitle: Best safety boots for concrete floors
pages.cardBlurb: Concrete's problem is fatigue, not impact — the cushioning-first spec that saves feet, knees and backs.
pages.h1: The best safety boots for concrete floors.
pages.metaTitle: Best Safety Boots for Concrete Floors | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Concrete floors punish feet through fatigue, not impact — the spec that matters: cushioned midsoles, energy-absorbing heels, replaced insoles and rotation, with the right S-code around it.
pages.lede: Ask what boot suits concrete and the honest answer starts with what concrete actually does: it returns every step's shock straight back up the leg, eight hours a day. The spec that matters isn't the toe cap — it's everything between your heel and the floor.

blocks.html:
Concrete's hazard isn't dramatic — it's cumulative: plantar fasciitis, knee and hip wear, lower-back fatigue, all downstream of a surface with zero give. Warehouse pickers, factory staff and workshop trades feel it as burning feet by hour six. The boot's job on concrete is shock management, and four features do it:

  • A genuinely cushioned midsole — EVA or PU foam with real depth, not a token layer under a rigid boot.
  • The energy-absorbing heel that's built into every code from S1 up — one reason plain SB boots are a false economy on hard floors.
  • A replaceable, cushioned insole — the component that actually dies first, and the cheapest to renew.
  • Weight discipline — every gram is lifted thousands of times a shift, which is why composite caps and trainer-style builds suit concrete so well.

The pick

rows: Light, foamy, midsole for stray fixings — the concrete default

blocks.html: Foam compresses; that's how it works and how it dies. The habits that keep concrete tolerable: replace insoles the moment they flatten (months, not years — a fresh insole revives a tired boot for a tenth of its price), rotate two pairs so the foam recovers between shifts, and retire on dead cushioning even when the uppers look fine — a boot that has stopped absorbing is transmitting. faq.q: What safety boots are best for standing on concrete all day?
faq.a: Cushioning-first builds: an S1P safety trainer or PU-midsole boot with a deep foam layer, energy-absorbing heel and a fresh replaceable insole — kept alive by rotating two pairs. The toe cap spec follows the job; the cushioning spec follows the floor.

faq.q: Why do my feet burn after a shift on concrete?
faq.a: Concrete returns every step's impact — burning feet, plantar fascia pain and knee fatigue are the cumulative result. Renewed insoles, genuinely cushioned midsoles, boot rotation and anti-fatigue matting at static posts each remove a share of the load.

faq.q: Are safety trainers OK on concrete floors?
faq.a: They're often the best choice — S1P trainers carry the same certified cap and midsole as boots with far less weight to lift each step, and their trainer-style foam handles concrete's shock better than many rigid boots. Step up to boots where ankle support or weather demands it.

pages.h1: How workwear embroidery pricing actually works.

pages.metaDesc: The workwear trade's embroidery pricing model explained honestly — why logos are usually included when you buy the garments, what the one-off digitising setup is, and when badging is charged separately.
pages.lede: Ask three suppliers what embroidery costs and you'll get 'free', a per-logo price and a shrug — and all three are describing the same model from different angles. Here's how the trade actually prices badged workwear, so you can compare quotes on the number that matters.

heroMeta.l: How the trade usually prices it

blocks.h2: "Free embroidery" is real — and priced in
blocks.html:
Most workwear suppliers, us included, quote badged garments as one price: buy the polos, the logo comes stitched. Nobody is donating machine time — the embroidery cost sits inside the garment price — but the bundling reflects something true about the work: once your logo is set up, running it onto a garment that's already passing through the workshop is efficient, so charging it as a separate line item mostly adds admin, not value.

The practical consequence for buyers: compare quotes on the total delivered price of the badged garment, not on whose line items say "free". A £9 polo with free embroidery and a £7 polo plus £2 per logo are the same quote wearing different clothes — and the garment quality, not the line-item theatre, is where the quotes genuinely differ (the polo guide covers what to look for).

blocks.h2: What actually moves an embroidery quote
blocks.html:
Stitch count is the honest unit of embroidery cost — driven by logo size and how much of it is solid fill. A clean left-chest logo of 8–10 cm runs quickly; a dense, fill-heavy crest at twice the size takes several times the machine minutes. Thread colour changes matter far less than people assume (multi-head machines carry many threads), and quantity matters the way you'd expect: the setup is fixed, so per-garment economics improve with volume — which is why suppliers can waive digitising on decent first orders.

Two more things worth knowing. Artwork quality is money: a crisp vector or high-resolution logo digitises cleanly; a stretched photo of a letterhead costs redraw time — one reason schools and clubs are told to treat the digitised crest as an asset they set up once and keep. And certified garments carry placement rules: badging hi-vis and FR kit must keep clear of the certified areas and use compatible processes — part of why safety kit gets badged by the workwear supplier, not the cheapest press in town.

faq.q: Why do workwear companies offer free embroidery?
faq.a: Because the trade bundles embroidery into the garment price — once a logo is digitised, stitching it onto garments already passing through the workshop is efficient, so most suppliers quote one badged-garment price. It's a pricing convention, not a giveaway: compare quotes on the total delivered price.

faq.q: What is a digitising fee?
faq.a: The one-off cost of converting your logo artwork into a machine stitch file — skilled work that determines how the logo renders in thread forever after. It's done once and reused across every garment and reorder; suppliers often waive it on larger first orders.

faq.q: Can I get my own garments embroidered?
faq.a: Yes — badging customer-supplied garments is standard work, and the route many schools and clubs use for existing kit. Expect it to be charged per logo rather than bundled, since there's no garment sale to absorb the cost, and note that certified hi-vis and FR items need placement-aware badging.

faq.q: What makes embroidery more expensive?
faq.a: Stitch count, mainly — bigger logos and dense solid fills take more machine time — plus extra positions per garment and per-unit personalisation like names. Thread colour count matters less than most buyers assume. Volume works the other way: fixed setup spread over more garments.

pages.lede: Front-of-house kit is the uniform customers actually look at — reception desks, restaurant floors, showrooms, salons. It has to read sharp at hour nine of a shift, wash at home without a dry-cleaning bill, and fit a team you didn't get to hand-pick. That's a different buying problem from a catalogue suit.

heroMeta.l: Tailoring or it costs you weekly

blocks.html:
The catalogue photo is not the test. The test is a receptionist's blouse after five wears and five washes, a maître d's jacket at the end of a double, a showroom skirt that's been sat down in two hundred times. Buy front-of-house kit on three questions: does it wash at home (dry-clean-only tailoring quietly adds hundreds a year per person), does it recover (crease-resistant and stretch fabrics read pressed at hour nine), and does the colour hold — because a faded navy next to a fresh navy looks worse than either alone.

Fabric answers most of it: poly-wool and technical poly blends for tailoring, polyester-rich blouse and dress cloths with a touch of elastane, and skirt weights heavy enough not to cling. Pure natural fibres look wonderful on day one and lose the plot by month three of commercial laundering.

One team, one palette: pick the colour story once and buy every garment — tailoring, blouses, dresses, skirts — inside it, so any mix on any body still reads as the same uniform.

faq.q: What fabric is best for front-of-house uniforms?
faq.a: Poly-wool or technical polyester blends with a small elastane content for tailoring, and easy-iron polyester-rich cloths for blouses and dresses. The blend does three jobs natural fibre can't sustain in shift work: home washability, crease recovery through a long day, and colour that stays matched across the team through repeat laundering.

faq.q: Should staff uniforms be dry-clean only?
faq.a: Avoid it wherever possible. Dry-clean-only tailoring either costs the business a recurring laundering bill or quietly stops being cleaned properly. Machine-washable suiting is widely available now and looks the part; specify it and the problem disappears at the buying stage.

faq.q: How do you keep a mixed team looking uniform?
faq.a: Fix the palette and buy every garment style inside it, from the same supplier range, so navy is the same navy across a suit, a dress and a skirt. Then offer real choice within the palette — trouser or skirt, dress or blouse, sleeve options — so people wear what suits them and everyone still matches.

faq.q: Is uniform for front-of-house staff tax deductible?
faq.a: For the employer, workwear provided to staff is a normal business expense. For employees required to wear and launder a recognisable uniform, HMRC's flat-rate uniform allowance may apply — see our uniform tax relief guide for how the claim works.

pages.cardTitle: Work headwear: caps, beanies and when it's PPE
pages.cardBlurb: Uniform caps, thermal beanies, bump caps and the line where headwear stops being branding and becomes protection.
pages.h1: Work headwear: uniform, warmth or PPE?
pages.metaTitle: Work Headwear Guide: Caps, Beanies, Bump Caps & Helmets | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Choosing work headwear — embroidered caps as uniform, thermal beanies for outdoor and cold-store work, EN 812 bump caps vs EN 397 helmets, and hygiene coverage for food environments.
pages.lede: Headwear is three different purchases wearing one name. Sometimes it's uniform — a logo cap on a delivery driver. Sometimes it's comfort kit — a thermal beanie on a winter site. And sometimes it's PPE with a standard number, where buying the wrong thing isn't a style mistake but a compliance one. Sort out which you're buying and the rest is easy.

heroMeta.l: Where the logo earns its keep

blocks.h2: Know which of the three you're buying
blocks.html:
Uniform headwear is branding: an embroidered cap puts the logo at eye level on every doorstep and counter, which is why couriers and trades franchises live in them. Buy on panel quality and embroidery position — a structured front panel takes a logo cleanly; unstructured caps crumple it.

Comfort headwear is thermal: beanies and liners for outdoor trades, cold stores and winter yards. Look for machine-washable acrylic or acrylic-wool, and thin-knit versions that fit under a helmet rather than instead of one.

Protective headwear carries a number. A bump cap (EN 812) protects against striking your own head on fixed objects — vans, low steel, plant interiors — and looks like a baseball cap with a shell inside. It is not a safety helmet: falling-object protection is EN 397 territory, decoded in our helmets guide. Sites that specify helmets mean helmets; a bump cap on a scaffold job is the wrong answer however smart it looks.

Food production adds a fourth, disposable case — hairnets, snoods and mob caps are hygiene consumables covered in our food processing guide.

faq.q: What is the difference between a bump cap and a safety helmet?
faq.a: A bump cap (EN 812) protects against you striking your head on fixed objects — low beams, vehicle interiors, racking. A safety helmet (EN 397) protects against falling objects and carries much higher impact requirements. They are not interchangeable: where a site or risk assessment specifies a helmet, a bump cap does not comply.

faq.q: Can you wear a beanie under a safety helmet?
faq.a: Yes, if it's a thin-knit or purpose-made helmet liner that doesn't interfere with the harness cradle. A thick beanie lifts the shell and changes how the helmet sits and performs. Many helmet ranges offer winter liners designed for exactly this.

faq.q: Where should a logo go on a work cap?
faq.a: Front and centre on a structured panel, typically around 55–65mm wide. Structured caps hold the embroidery flat; unstructured ones crease through the design. Keep the artwork simple — fine text disappears at cap-embroidery scale.

pages.cardTitle: Choosing a work jacket: shell, softshell, insulated or gilet
pages.cardBlurb: The four jacket families, what each is actually for, and the layering logic that stops you buying warmth you can't work in.
pages.h1: Choosing a work jacket, family first.
pages.metaTitle: Work Jacket Guide: Shell vs Softshell vs Insulated vs Gilet | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How to choose a work jacket — waterproof shells and EN 343, softshells for everyday wind and showers, insulated jackets for static cold work, and gilets for active jobs that need a free arm swing.
pages.lede: Jacket regret is nearly always a category mistake, not a quality one: a waterproof bought for warmth, a padded jacket sweated through by an active job, a fleece facing January rain. Pick the family first — shell, softshell, insulated, or gilet — and almost any decent garment inside it will do its job.

blocks.html:
Everything follows from how the job generates heat. Active work — carrying, climbing, fitting, delivering — makes its own warmth and needs a jacket that manages weather without cooking you: a softshell for everyday wind and drizzle, a true waterproof shell when it's properly raining (the rating system is decoded in our EN 343 guide), or a gilet when the arms need to swing free and the core just needs cover.

Static work — banksman duties, gate security, machine minding, cold-store picking — generates almost nothing, and that's where insulated jackets and parkas earn their bulk. The classic mistake runs both directions: padded jackets on active jobs end up tied round waists by ten o'clock, and softshells on static winter jobs are a misery by lunch.

Layers beat bulk either way: a base layer and a mid-layer under a shell covers more conditions than one heavyweight jacket ever will — and when the choice inside a family is genuinely close, our softshell vs fleece comparison settles the commonest one.

faq.q: What's the difference between a softshell and a waterproof jacket?
faq.a: A softshell is wind-resistant and shower-resistant — ideal for active work in everyday weather — but its fabric and seams are not sealed. A waterproof shell carries an EN 343 rating with taped seams and keeps sustained rain out for a full shift. If the forecast says rain all day, it's a shell job.

faq.q: Are bodywarmers any good for work?
faq.a: Excellent for active jobs: they keep the core warm while leaving the arms completely free, which is why fitters, couriers and warehouse teams favour them. They're core-only warmth though — in real cold they work as a layer over knitwear or under a shell, not alone.

faq.q: Can you embroider a waterproof jacket?
faq.a: Yes, but embroidery needles puncture the waterproof membrane, so it needs doing properly — sealed behind the stitching or applied to a bonded patch. It's standard practice for a competent workwear embroiderer; just don't have a fashion embroiderer do it as if it were a hoodie.

faq.q: What jacket is best for standing outside all day?
faq.a: An insulated jacket or parka sized over a base and mid-layer, with sealed cuffs and a decent hem drop. Static outdoor work generates almost no body heat, so buy for insulation and wind-proofing rather than breathability — the opposite of what an active trade needs.

pages.cardTitle: Women's workwear: fit is a safety issue
pages.cardBlurb: Unisex means men's — and ill-fitting kit isn't just uncomfortable, it protects worse. What to demand instead.
pages.h1: Women's workwear: 'unisex' is doing a lot of lifting.
pages.metaTitle: Women's Workwear Guide: Fit, PPE Sizing & What To Demand | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Women's workwear done properly — why unisex kit is men's kit resized, how bad fit degrades protection (gloves, hi-vis, harnesses), what women's-cut ranges actually change, and how to order for a mixed team.
pages.lede: A third of many site and healthcare teams are women wearing kit patterned on men — sleeves rolled twice, gloves a size too big, hi-vis like a tabard on a fence post. That's not a comfort niggle: excess fabric snags, oversized gloves fumble, and PPE that doesn't fit doesn't protect as certified. The fix exists; you just have to specify it.

heroMeta.l: PPE certifies on a fitted body
Women's kit is repatterned, not resized

heroImage.alt: Lilac maternity scrub top with gathered bump panel

blocks.html:
Unisex workwear is drafted on a male block: straighter hip, longer torso, broader shoulder, bigger hands. Put it on a typical female frame and the failures are physical, not aesthetic — trousers that gape or won't rise, excess sleeve and jacket fabric that catches on machinery and ladders, gloves whose empty fingertips wreck dexterity and get deliberately removed, and hi-vis that drapes so the retroreflective bands sit wrong. Safety kit is tested and certified on the assumption it fits; oversized isn't a style, it's a derating.

What a real women's range changes: repatterned rise and hip on trousers, shorter back length and adjusted shoulder on jackets, narrower lasts on safety boots, and gloves in genuine small sizes with proportionate finger lengths — not the same garment graded down. Maternity is its own list, covered in our maternity guide.

faq.q: Is women's workwear actually different or just smaller?
faq.a: Properly made women's ranges are repatterned — different rise and hip on trousers, adjusted shoulder and back length on jackets, narrower boot lasts, proportionate glove fingers — not men's garments graded down. That drafting difference is what makes the kit sit, move and protect correctly.

faq.q: Does badly fitting PPE really reduce protection?
faq.a: Yes. Gloves with empty fingertips destroy dexterity and get removed; excess jacket and sleeve fabric snags on machinery and ladders; draped hi-vis mispositions its reflective bands; boots on the wrong last cause the blisters that put people in trainers. PPE is certified assuming correct fit — oversized quietly voids the assumption.

faq.q: Do employers have to provide women's-fit PPE?
faq.a: Employers must provide PPE that fits and suits each wearer — supplying men's sizing only and calling it unisex doesn't meet that duty where fit is compromised. Women's-cut options now exist across nearly every category, so availability is rarely a defensible objection.

pages.cardTitle: Summer workwear: heat, UV and the shorts question
pages.cardBlurb: Wicking fabrics, UPF, hi-vis in a heatwave and what sites actually say about shorts — the hot-weather kit list.
pages.h1: Summer workwear: staying safe when the site bakes.
pages.metaTitle: Summer Workwear Guide: Heat, UV Protection & Site Rules | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Hot-weather workwear that works — wicking fabrics vs cotton, UPF sun protection for outdoor trades, hi-vis compliance in summer, the shorts-on-site question and heat-stress basics.
pages.lede: British summers are short and increasingly brutal, and outdoor trades feel every degree. Hot-weather kit is a genuine safety topic — heat stress degrades judgement before it drops anyone, and UV is a career-length skin-cancer dose for outdoor workers — but most of the fixes are fabric choices, made in advance.

heroMeta.l: Fabric that moves sweat beats less fabric
Sun protection you wear, not reapply
Shorts are a policy, not a right

blocks.h2: Less clothing isn't the win it feels like
blocks.html:
The instinct in a heatwave is minimum fabric; the physiology disagrees. Bare skin in direct sun gains radiant heat and UV dose; what actually cools is evaporation — which a lightweight wicking synthetic accelerates by spreading sweat, while a soaked cotton tee just sits wet and heavy against the skin. So summer buying is fabric-first: wicking tees and polos, lighter-gsm trousers with stretch and venting, and technical base layers that do in July what they do in January — move moisture.

Sun is the quieter hazard. Outdoor workers carry multiples of the general population's UV exposure, and long sleeves in light wicking fabric with a UPF rating beat sunscreen's reapply-every-two-hours reality for arms and shoulders. Neck flaps and brims on headwear cover the spots that burn first.

faq.q: Can you wear shorts on a construction site?
faq.a: Only if the site allows it — many don't, citing impact and abrasion risk, UV exposure and task hazards, and some allow them only for specific trades or with specific risk assessments. It's a site policy question, not a legal entitlement either way. Lightweight stretch trousers are the compromise that usually survives the argument.

faq.q: What's the best fabric for working in hot weather?
faq.a: Lightweight moisture-wicking synthetics (or technical blends) that spread sweat and let it evaporate — evaporation is what cools you. Heavy cotton feels natural but holds sweat against the skin. For sun exposure, light long sleeves with a UPF rating often beat bare arms on both comfort and dose.

faq.q: Do hi-vis rules relax in summer?
faq.a: No — if the risk assessment says Class 2 or 3, it says so in August. The answer is summer-weight hi-vis: mesh-backed vests, lightweight polos and jackets certified to the same EN ISO 20471 classes. Compliance and comfort aren't in conflict once you buy for the season.

pages.cardTitle: Apprentice kit: what to buy before day one
pages.cardBlurb: What a first-year actually needs, what the employer must provide free, and where a tight budget should go first.

pages.lede: Every September a wave of first-years turns up to site, workshop and kitchen in kit bought hopefully the weekend before — some of it wrong, some of it wasted, some of it stuff the employer was legally obliged to provide anyway. Here's the honest split: what to buy, what to wait for, and where the budget goes first.

Specialist kit comes with the job

blocks.h2: What you buy vs what they provide
blocks.html:
Clear the biggest confusion first: PPE that a risk assessment requires must be provided free by the employer — hard hats, required hi-vis, task gloves, eye and hearing protection, FR, and in most cases safety footwear where it's mandated. The full position is in who pays for PPE. What apprentices genuinely end up buying is the workwear around it: trousers, tees, mid-layers, and often a first pair of boots before the employer's arrangements kick in.

So before spending: ask the employer or training provider for the kit list. A good one tells you exactly what's issued and what's yours. The list below covers the near-universal personal buys.

faq.q: Do apprentices have to buy their own PPE?
faq.a: No — PPE required by the risk assessment must be provided free of charge by the employer, apprentice or not. What apprentices commonly do buy is general workwear (trousers, tees, layers) and sometimes a first pair of safety boots before employer arrangements kick in. Ask for the kit list before spending anything.

faq.q: What safety boots should an apprentice buy?
faq.a: A well-fitting S1P or S3 boot from a reputable maker — S3 if the work is outdoors in mud, S1P often suffices indoors. Fit beats features: try them on late in the day, walk properly, and spend what you can afford here rather than on logo tees. Your feet do every shift of a forty-year career.

faq.q: How much does starter workwear cost?
faq.a: A sensible day-one bundle — boots, two work trousers, four or five tees, a mid-layer, a waterproof and basics — is typically low hundreds of pounds, with boots rightly the biggest single line. Buy the cheap items cheap and the boots good; upgrade everything else as the trade teaches you what it eats.

pages.cardTitle: Workwear fabrics explained: gsm, blends and weaves
pages.cardBlurb: What 245gsm polycotton actually tells you — the fabric literacy that makes every other buying decision easier.
pages.h1: Workwear fabrics: learn to read the cloth.
pages.metaTitle: Workwear Fabrics Explained: GSM, Polycotton & Weaves | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Workwear fabric literacy — what gsm weights mean, polycotton ratios, ripstop and canvas weaves, stretch content, and how fabric choice drives durability, comfort and washing behaviour.
pages.lede: Every garment listing leads with a number and a blend — 245gsm 65/35 polycotton — that most buyers skim past. It's the most information-dense line on the page: weight, fibre and weave predict how a garment wears, washes, breathes and dies. Ten minutes of fabric literacy upgrades every order you'll ever place.

heroMeta.l: Grams per square metre — the weight

blocks.h2: Weight, fibre, weave — in that order
blocks.html:
GSM is fabric weight, and weight predicts character: 140–180gsm is shirt and summer-polo territory; 200–260gsm is the workwear heartland (trousers, polos, sweats that survive trade use); 300gsm+ is heavy canvas and winter fleece — durable, warm, slow to dry. Heavier isn't better, it's slower and tougher: a 320gsm trouser outlasts a 240 but punishes an August loft.

Fibre is the blend line. Cotton brings comfort, breathability and easy dyeing; polyester brings strength, colourfastness, fast drying and crease recovery. The 65/35 polycotton ratio dominates workwear because it takes cotton's feel and polyester's survival; reversed ratios (35/65) push durability further for washing-heavy fleets — the reason industrially launderable garments lean polyester-rich. Pure cotton keeps two specialist thrones: comfort against skin, and — critically — it doesn't melt, which is why heat trades and FR underlayers care (synthetics near flame melt onto skin; the reason polyester tees under FR are banned). A few percent elastane buys the stretch modern trousers are loved for — at a price in heat tolerance and tumble-dryer life.

Weave finishes the prediction: twill is the standard workwear weave (diagonal grain, drapes and wears well); canvas is the stiff heavy-duty version; ripstop grids reinforcing threads so tears stop at the box — lighter fabrics acting tougher, the summer-trouser trick.

faq.q: What does gsm mean in clothing?
faq.a: Grams per square metre — the fabric's weight. Workwear mostly lives between 200 and 260gsm; lighter means cooler and faster-drying, heavier means tougher and warmer. It's the quickest single predictor of how a garment will feel and last.

faq.q: Is polycotton better than cotton for workwear?
faq.a: For most work, yes — the 65/35 blend keeps much of cotton's comfort while adding polyester's strength, colourfastness and crease recovery, and it survives repeated washing far better. Pure cotton keeps the advantage for comfort against skin and around heat, because it doesn't melt.

faq.q: What is ripstop fabric?
faq.a: A weave with a grid of reinforcing threads so that tears stop at the next grid line instead of running. It lets lighter, cooler fabrics behave more toughly — the classic construction for summer-weight work trousers and outdoor kit.

pages.cardTitle: Winter workwear: the layering buy
pages.cardBlurb: Base, mid, shell and extremities — buying winter kit as a system, with the standards that matter when it's properly cold.
pages.h1: Winter workwear: buy the system, not the coat.
pages.metaTitle: Winter Workwear Guide: Layering, Standards & Kit List | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Winter workwear bought properly — the three-layer system, when EN 342 certification matters, hands and head as the real weak points, and the wet-cold reality of British winters.
pages.lede: The British winter injury isn't frostbite — it's the productivity and judgement drain of being wet-cold for six hours, plus the hands that stop working first. Winter buying that starts with 'a big coat' solves the wrong problem: the right purchase is a system whose layers come on and off as the work heats up.

blocks.html:
Base moves sweat — because active work generates moisture in any temperature, and wet skin in cold air is how the misery starts. Wicking synthetics or merino; never cotton against winter skin (the full base-layer logic). Mid holds warmth — fleece, insulated gilets or knits, sized to the person's heat output: the scaffolder and the gate guard need different thicknesses of the same idea. Shell stops weather — wind first (windchill does more daily damage than temperature), rain always (EN 343 ratings decoded), and it must fit over the other layers, which is why winter shells are bought a size wiser (the jacket families).

When certification enters: ordinary winter work is layering judgement, but static work in real cold — gates, banksman duties, and everything in cold stores — moves to EN 342-rated ensembles with measured insulation. And extremities decide the day: EN 511 gloves (the wet-cold test matters more than the temperature one in Britain), thermal socks that still fit inside the boot, and a beanie or helmet liner — the cheapest warmth per pound anywhere on the body.

faq.q: What should you wear for outdoor work in winter?
faq.a: A three-layer system: wicking base (never cotton), insulating mid sized to your work rate, and a windproof, waterproof shell sized to fit over both — plus EN 511-rated gloves with spares, thermal socks and head coverage. Layers beat one heavy coat because effort varies through the shift.

faq.q: When is EN 342 clothing needed?
faq.a: For sustained work in genuinely cold environments — cold stores and freezer chambers above all, plus very cold static outdoor roles. EN 342 ensembles carry measured insulation values rather than 'padded' promises. Ordinary winter site work is served by good layering without the certification.

faq.q: Why do hands fail first in winter work?
faq.a: Fingers have high surface area, low muscle mass and get wet — and once dexterity drops, the work stops or gets dangerous. EN 511-rated gloves (tested for wet and convective cold), dry spares in the van and glove discipline outperform any amount of extra jacket.

pages.lede: Some jobs are simply too wet, too washed-down or too biologically interesting for leather boots — and for them the safety wellington is the real spec, not the compromise. The buying decisions are few but they compound: code, material, and the fit that survives a thermal sock.

blocks.h2: S4, S5 and the material question
blocks.html:
The code ladder gives wellingtons two rungs: S4 — waterproof polymer boot with 200 J toe cap, antistatic, energy-absorbing heel — and S5, which adds the penetration-resistant midsole and cleated outsole. The choice mirrors S1P-vs-S3 logic: S4 for wet-clean environments (food halls, dairies, washdown lines), S5 wherever the ground can bite back — farmyards, construction groundwork, wet chambers, waste sites.

Material is the underrated decision. PVC boots are the cheap end: heavier, stiffer, colder, and they crack at the flex point sooner. Polyurethane (PU) costs more and repays it daily: roughly a third lighter, flexible in cold that turns PVC rigid, better insulated, and typically two to three times the working life — the cost-per-month arithmetic embarrasses the bargain boot. Food and agri sectors standardised on PU years ago for exactly this reason. Fit note: wellingtons are worn with thick or thermal socks most of the year — size for that sock, check calf clearance over work trousers, and prefer models with a proper heel kick for muddy removal.

faq.q: What is the difference between S4 and S5 wellingtons?
faq.a: Both are waterproof safety wellingtons with a 200 J toe cap; S5 adds a penetration-resistant midsole and cleated outsole. Wet-clean indoor environments suit S4; anywhere with debris, mud or unknown ground underfoot — farms, sites, waste — wants S5.

faq.q: Are polyurethane wellingtons worth the extra cost?
faq.a: Almost always: PU boots are significantly lighter, stay flexible in cold, insulate better and typically last two to three times as long as PVC — so the cost per month of wear usually favours them despite the higher price. Full-time wellington wearers feel the difference by mid-morning.

faq.q: How should safety wellingtons fit?
faq.a: Sized for the thick or thermal socks you'll actually wear, with room to wiggle toes clear of the cap, calf clearance over work trousers, and a snug enough instep that the boot doesn't pump when walking. A heel kick plate matters more than it sounds — muddy removal is a daily event.

pages.cardTitle: Embroidery artwork: designing a logo that stitches
pages.cardBlurb: Why some logos embroider beautifully and others turn to mush — the artwork rules that decide it before the first stitch.
pages.h1: Logos that stitch: the artwork rules.
pages.metaTitle: Embroidery Artwork Guide: Designing Logos That Stitch Well | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: What makes a logo embroider well — minimum text sizes, detail limits, colour and gradient realities, placement sizing, and how to prepare artwork so digitising goes right first time.
pages.lede: Embroidery is drawing with a needle that refuses to draw anything smaller than a stitch. Most disappointing logo results were decided before the machine started — in artwork with hairline details, six-point text and gradients thread can't make. Here's what survives the needle, and how to prepare for it.

heroImage.alt: Multi-head embroidery machine stitching a logo

blocks.h2: What thread can and can't do
blocks.html:
The needle's alphabet has minimums: text below roughly 4–5 mm tall fills in and blurs — the registered-trademark symbol and web addresses are the classic casualties; fine lines below about a millimetre disappear or bulge; gradients don't exist in thread — a fade becomes stepped bands of solid colour, which a good digitiser designs deliberately or (better) the artwork avoids; and large solid fills get heavy, stiff and pucker-prone on light garments — outlines and partial fills wear better. Colour is genuinely excellent news: thread colour is vivid and permanent, standard palettes match most brand colours closely, and a dozen colours cost no more to run than two (the machine just changes thread).

The digitising step is where quality lives: converting artwork to a stitch file is a craft decision about stitch types, directions, densities and underlay per fabric — which is why the same logo needs adjusting between a stable twill and a stretchy pique, and why the digitised file, done once and kept, is what guarantees every future batch matches (the one-off cost our pricing guide explains). Supply the cleanest artwork you own — vector (.ai/.eps/.svg) ideally, or the largest sharp image — plus brand colour references, and say which garments it's going on.

faq.q: What file format is best for embroidery?
faq.a: Vector formats (.ai, .eps, .svg, or vector PDF) digitise cleanest because every shape is mathematically defined. Failing that, the largest, sharpest raster image you have. The digitiser converts it once into a stitch file, which is then reused identically for every future order.

faq.q: Why does small text embroider badly?
faq.a: A stitch has physical width — below roughly 4–5 mm letter height, letterforms fill in and read as texture rather than text. Straplines, web addresses and ® symbols are the usual casualties; the fix is dropping or enlarging them in the workwear version of the logo.

faq.q: Can embroidery do gradients?
faq.a: Not literally — thread is solid colour. Digitisers can suggest gradients with stepped bands or directional stitching, but the honest answer is to redesign fades as solid zones for the stitched version. Most brands run a simplified 'embroidery version' of their logo for exactly this reason.

pages.cardTitle: Coveralls: the buying guide
pages.cardBlurb: Standard, FR, chemical or disposable — the one-garment wardrobe sorted by job, fit and the details that matter in wear.
pages.h1: Coveralls: one garment, four families.
pages.metaTitle: Coveralls Buying Guide: Standard, FR, Chem & Disposable | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Coverall buying decoded — the four families (standard, FR multi-norm, chemical, disposable), fit rules for a garment you bend in all day, and the details (zips, access, knees) that separate good from cheap.
pages.lede: The coverall is workwear's one-decision wardrobe: a single garment covering torso to ankle, bought by trades from mechanics to turnaround crews. The four families answer different questions — everyday cover, flame, chemistry, or single-use — and inside each, the difference between good and irritating is a handful of construction details.

heroMeta.l: Size for the crouch, not the stand
Zips and access make or break it

blocks.html:
Standard coveralls — 245–300gsm polycotton, the garage and workshop default — are bought on fit and details (below), in rotation quantities because oil retires them chemically. FR and multi-norm coveralls are certification purchases: EN ISO 11612 letters for heat and flame, welding spec, or the refinery triple of FR + antistatic + splash — the label list is the product. Chemical coveralls run the type ladder from type 6 splash upward. Disposables — type 5/6 for dust and light splash — are consumables bought by the case, covered honestly in the disposables guide.

Fit is the coverall's make-or-break: the garment must accommodate a crouch, a reach and a crawl simultaneously — which is why the fit test is squatting, not standing. Look for a generous back rise or bi-swing back, and size over what's worn beneath in winter. The details that separate good from cheap: a two-way zip (ventilation and, frankly, plumbing), covered stud plackets that don't scratch paintwork, knee-pad pockets in trade versions, elasticated waist panels, and pocket access slits that reach the trousers underneath — the feature nobody notices until they've lived without it.

faq.q: How should a coverall fit?
faq.a: Test it crouching, not standing: squat, reach overhead and cross your arms — the garment should follow without pulling at the crotch or shoulders. Size to wear over your normal work layers, and prefer bi-swing backs and stretch panels for mobile trades.

faq.q: What is a multi-norm coverall?
faq.a: A garment certified to several protective standards at once — typically flame resistance (EN ISO 11612), antistatic performance (EN 1149-5) and chemical splash (EN 13034), sometimes with welding or arc ratings. Process sites specify them because layering separate single-purpose garments gets the protection wrong.

faq.q: Why do coveralls have a two-way zip?
faq.a: Ventilation from the bottom when working hot, and practical access without undressing — both daily realities in a one-piece garment. It's one of the small construction details (with covered plackets, knee-pad pockets and pass-through pockets) that separate a good coverall from a cheap one.

pages.cardTitle: Women's safety boots: lasts, not labels
pages.cardBlurb: Why 'small men's sizes' cause the blisters — what a women's last changes, and how to buy boots that actually fit.
pages.h1: Women's safety boots: the last matters most.
pages.metaTitle: Women's Safety Boots Guide: Fit, Lasts & Buying Advice | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Women's safety boots explained — why downsized men's boots cause heel slip and blisters, what a women's last changes (heel, width, volume), the codes that stay identical, and buying advice that works.
pages.lede: The most common women's safety-boot experience is a size 5 men's boot, a heel that lifts with every step, and blisters by Wednesday — followed by trainers on Thursday, which is how bad fit becomes a safety incident. The fix isn't a smaller boot; it's a boot built on a different shape.

heroMeta.l: Heel, width and volume — not just length
The tell of a men's boot downsized

blocks.html:
A boot is built around a last — the foot-shaped form that sets its internal geometry — and a typical women's foot differs from a scaled-down men's foot in ways length can't fix: narrower heel relative to the forefoot (the anatomical mismatch behind heel slip), lower instep volume (why downsized boots feel cavernous however tight the laces), and different proportions through the arch. Put a female foot in a small men's last and the heel pistons, friction builds, blisters follow — and lacing harder just moves the pain. A women's-last boot changes the shape, not just the size, and the difference is felt in the first hundred metres.

What doesn't change: the certification. Women's-last boots carry the same S1P/S3 codes, the same 200 J caps and midsoles (2022 codes included). Availability has genuinely improved — proper ranges exist across site boots, trainers and wellingtons — so the fallback of 'we could only get men's' rarely survives an actual search, and the fit-is-safety argument gives the buying meeting its teeth. Buying advice that works: try boots late in the day (feet swell), in the socks you'll wear, and judge heel hold walking on an incline if you can find one — that's where slip announces itself.

faq.q: Are women's safety boots just small men's boots?
faq.a: Good ones aren't — they're built on women's lasts with a narrower heel-to-forefoot ratio and lower instep volume, which is what stops heel slip and blistering. Downsized men's boots keep men's proportions and cause most of the fit misery women report in safety footwear.

faq.q: Are women's safety boots as protective as men's?
faq.a: Identical where the codes match — S1P is S1P and S3 is S3 regardless of last, with the same 200-joule toe caps and midsole tests. The certification doesn't distinguish; only the internal shape does.

faq.q: What if my employer only stocks men's sizes?
faq.a: PPE must fit the wearer — supplying only men's-last footwear doesn't meet that duty when fit is compromised, and women's-last ranges are now genuinely available across boot types. Raise it with the fit-is-safety argument; it's an ordering change, not a special request.

pages.cardTitle: Tall and plus-size workwear: fit at the range edges
pages.cardBlurb: Leg lengths, extended sizes and the PPE that must still fit at 5XL — buying properly for the ends of the size curve.
pages.h1: Workwear at the edges of the size range.
pages.metaTitle: Tall & Plus-Size Workwear Guide: Extended Sizing Done Right | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Tall and plus-size workwear buying — leg-length options, extended chest sizes, why hi-vis class and harness fit change at large sizes, and how employers order for the whole real workforce.
pages.lede: Every workforce has bodies the standard size run ignores — the 6'5" engineer whose trousers are ankle-swingers, the 5XL operative whose hi-vis won't close and therefore doesn't protect. Buying at the range edges isn't a favour; it's the same fit-equals-function rule everywhere else, applied where catalogues go quiet.

heroMeta.l: Real ranges reach further than habit
An open hi-vis isn't Class anything

blocks.h2: What actually goes wrong at the edges
blocks.html:
Tall problems are length problems: trousers riding above the boot (and dragging the knee-pad pocket off the knee — the pad protects a shin instead), sleeves exposing wrists to weather and spatter, jackets that untuck at every reach. Most trade ranges cut short/regular/tall legs and some cut tall bodies — the failure is usually ordering habit, not availability. Plus-size problems are protection problems: a hi-vis that can't close loses its certified area the moment it flaps open (class is area maths); stretch panels and correct sizing keep outer layers actually closable over winter mid-layers; and harness-based work needs rated, sized fall-protection equipment — standard harnesses have weight and girth limits, and exceeding them is an equipment-selection issue the employer must solve, not a squeeze-it-on issue (see the fall-protection map).

For employers the fix is procedural: collect real measurements at intake (our measuring guide makes it a five-minute job), order the size curve you actually employ rather than a bell curve from habit, and pick core ranges that genuinely extend — same garment, same colour, 3XS to 5XL+ with leg options — so nobody's uniform announces them as an afterthought. That last point is the quiet one: matching kit at every size is a dignity feature, and it costs nothing but supplier choice.

faq.q: Does workwear come in tall sizes?
faq.a: Most serious trade ranges cut short, regular and tall leg lengths and some cut tall body lengths — the gap is usually in ordering habits rather than catalogues. Per-person leg length matters functionally: knee-pad pockets only protect knees they actually sit on.

faq.q: Why does hi-vis fit matter at larger sizes?
faq.a: Because the class rating is certified area, worn as designed — a garment that can't close and flaps open no longer presents its certified fluorescent and reflective area. Extended-size hi-vis that closes properly over real layers is the compliant answer, and it exists.

faq.q: Are there weight limits on safety harnesses?
faq.a: Yes — harnesses and energy-absorbing systems carry rated capacity limits, and standard models don't fit or protect every body. Where height work is involved, equipment selection for larger workers is a competent-person decision with properly rated, sized kit — never an improvised fit.

pages.cardTitle: Workwear sizing: how to measure
pages.cardBlurb: Five measurements, five minutes, no returns — the measuring routine that makes team orders arrive right first time.
pages.h1: How to measure for workwear that fits first time.
pages.metaTitle: Workwear Sizing Guide: How To Measure Properly | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How to measure for workwear — chest, waist, inside leg, and the rules that stop returns: measure the body not the old garment, size for layers, and read each maker's chart because sizes aren't standard.
pages.lede: Half of all workwear returns are self-inflicted: sizes guessed from a favourite tee, waists quoted from denial, one 'L' assumed to equal another. The cure is five measurements taken in five minutes with a fabric tape — and the two rules that turn them into garments that fit on arrival.

heroMeta.l: Chest, waist, hip, inside leg, collar
Measure the body, not old clothes

steps.name: Chest
steps.text: Tape around the fullest part of the chest, under the arms, level across the back — snug, not compressed, arms relaxed at the sides.

steps.name: Waist
steps.text: Around the natural waist where trousers actually sit — over a shirt is fine, breathe normally, no tape-tightening optimism. Work trousers are worn loaded; honest beats aspirational.

steps.name: Hip / seat
steps.text: Around the fullest part of the seat, feet together — the number that decides whether trousers accommodate a crouch.

steps.name: Inside leg
steps.text: From crotch seam to where the trouser should end — the boot's ankle cuff — measured against a well-fitting trouser laid flat if easier. Order short/regular/tall accordingly.

steps.name: Collar (for shirts)
steps.text: Around the base of the neck with one finger inside the tape — the finger is the comfort allowance.

blocks.html:
Rule one: measure the body, not the wardrobe. A favourite old garment has stretched, shrunk and been chosen for reasons memory flatters; the tape hasn't. (Workwear sizing is also honest by regulation — EN ISO 13688 requires declared sizes to map to body dimensions — so honest inputs meet honest labels.)

Rule two: read the maker's chart, every time. Sizes are not standardised across brands — one maker's L is another's XL, and workwear cuts vary deliberately (a coverall allows for layers and crouching; a softshell doesn't). Match your numbers to each chart rather than transferring letters between brands. Two refinements finish the job: size outer layers over what's actually worn beneath (the winter-shell rule from the layering guide), and for teams, collect measurements at intake rather than asking people to shout sizes across a yard — it's quicker than one exchange paperwork cycle, and it feeds the quantity maths a real size curve, including the range edges.

faq.q: How do you measure chest size for workwear?
faq.a: Tape around the fullest part of the chest, under the arms and level across the back, snug but not compressed, with arms relaxed. Match that number to the specific maker's size chart — letters like L and XL aren't standardised between brands.

faq.q: Should workwear be a size bigger?
faq.a: Not as a rule — modern workwear is cut for work, including layering allowances where relevant. The exceptions are deliberate: outer shells sized over real underlayers, and coveralls tested in a crouch. Otherwise measure honestly and follow the chart; oversizing creates its own snag and drape problems.

faq.q: How should companies collect staff sizes?
faq.a: Measure at intake with a fabric tape — five measurements per person, five minutes — rather than collecting self-declared letters. It feeds orders a real size curve including tall legs and extended sizes, and it costs less than one round of exchange postage.
